newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean bankers arrested in growing loan scandal.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean bankers arrested in growing loan scandal.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors arrested two leading bankers on Wednesday and a prominent opposition parliamentarian said he had taken money from the man at the centre of a loan scandal involving the Hanbo Group.
A prosecution spokesman said Sheen Kwang-shik, president of Korea First Bank, and Woo Chan-mok, head of Cho Hung Bank, were arrested on charges of bribery and taken to a Seoul prison.
Prosecutors accused Sheen and Woo of taking 400 million won ($460,000) each from Chung Tae-soo, founder of the troubled Hanbo Group, in return for huge loans from the two banks.

The move follows the arrest last Friday of Chung, who was still being questioned by prosecutors on whether he provided kickbacks to other bankers or politicians, senior prosecutor Choi Byung-koog said.

Korea First and Cho Hung, along with the state-run Korea Development Bank, are the main creditors of Hanbo Steel, which racked up about five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans before it was declared insolvent on January 23.

In a fresh twist to the scandal, lawmaker Kwon Roh-kap, a close associate of opposition leader Kim Dae-jung, said he had accepted between 150 million and 160 million won ($173,000 and $184,000) from Chung, partly to fund an election campaign.
Kim Dae-jung, who heads the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, has accused the government of peddling influence for the massive loans to Hanbo Steel.

Asked by reporters on Wednesday about the nature of the money he received from Chung, Kwon said: "I believe they were either political funds or rice cake money. But I have nothing to do with preferential lendings to Hanbo."
South Koreans traditionally swap small amounts of money, known as rice cake money, or gifts during major holidays as a token of friendship or respect.
Kwon said part of the money was used to finance a party election in 1993.

He is the first politician to admit taking money from Chung, who built up South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate by rapidly expanding the steelmaking flagship and acquiring or setting up 18 companies over the past three years.
Political analysts said with presidential elections only 10 months away, the Hanbo scandal could have a serious impact on the polls.
"The ruling and opposition parties appeared to be poised to wage a smear campaign against each other," said Cho Chang-hyun, political science professor at Hanyang University.
"No one in South Korea believes such huge loans are possible without political pressure. Public attention would now be focused on which powerful figures exercised influence," Cho said.
President Kim, who ordered a probe into the loans last week, has called the scandal a typical example of corruption.

Since taking office in 1993, the president has worked hard to build a reputation as an anti-graft crusader but his image has been hurt over the past year by the arrest of several of his top officials, including a defence minister, on bribery charges.
He also suffered a humiliating climbdown over a new labour law which was sent back to parliament after four weeks of industrial strife.
Apart from Sheen and Woo, prosecutors also questioned Lee Hyung-koo, former chief of the state Korea Development Bank, but allowed him to return home, senior prosecutor Choi said.
State prosecutors have questioned officials of Hanbo and its creditor banks over a lobbying fund kept by Chung and examined the conglomerate's bank accounts to check for irregularities.
